claim: Genome-wide association studies (GWASs) for bone mineral density (BMD) in humans have identified over 1100 associations to date.
source: Genome-wide association studies (GWASs) for bone mineral density (BMD) in humans have identified over 1100 associations to date.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Morris et al., 2019 in the manuscript context.

claim: Identifying causal genes implicated by GWAS studies has been challenging.
source: However, identifying causal genes implicated by such studies has been challenging.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by the broader scientific literature context.

claim: The study identified 512 genes as significant using both TWAS and eQTL colocalization.
source: Using this approach, we identified 512 genes as significant using both TWAS and eQTL colocalization.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis, supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The set of 512 genes was enriched for regulators of BMD and members of bone relevant biological processes.
source: This set of genes was enriched for regulators of BMD and members of bone relevant biological processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: PPP6R3 was the gene with the strongest support from the analysis which was not previously implicated in the regulation of BMD.
source: To investigate the significance of our findings, we selected PPP6R3, the gene with the strongest support from our analysis which was not previously implicated in the regulation of BMD, for further investigation.
evidence: This is based on the ranking of genes by TWAS p-value and colocalization scores, as shown in Table 2.

claim: Ppp6r3 deletion in mice decreased BMD.
source: We observed that Ppp6r3 deletion in mice decreased BMD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Ppp6r3 knockout mice presented in Figure 4.

claim: Osteoporosis affects over 10 million individuals in the United States.
source: Osteoporosis, a disease characterized by low bone mineral density (BMD), decreased bone strength, and an increased risk of fracture, affects over 10 million individuals in the United States (Black and Rosen, 2016; Burge et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Black and Rosen, 2016 and Burge et al., 2007.

claim: BMD is the single strongest predictor of fracture.
source: BMD is the single strongest predictor of fracture and a highly heritable quantitative trait (Miller et al., 1999; Ralston and Uitterlinden, 2010; Peacock et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Miller et al., 1999; Ralston and Uitterlinden, 2010; Peacock et al., 2002.

claim: BMD is a highly heritable quantitative trait.
source: BMD is the single strongest predictor of fracture and a highly heritable quantitative trait (Miller et al., 1999; Ralston and Uitterlinden, 2010; Peacock et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Miller et al., 1999; Ralston and Uitterlinden, 2010; Peacock et al., 2002.

claim: Over the last decade, genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have identified over 1100 independent associations for BMD.
source: Over the last decade, genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have identified over 1100 independent associations for BMD (Morris et al., 2019; Estrada et al., 2012; Kemp et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Morris et al., 2019; Estrada et al., 2012; Kemp et al., 2017.

claim: Despite the success of GWAS, few of the underlying causal genes have been identified.
source: However, despite the success of GWAS, few of the underlying causal genes have been identified (Rocha-Braz and Ferraz-de-Souza, 2016; Sabik and Farber, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rocha-Braz and Ferraz-de-Souza, 2016; Sabik and Farber, 2017.

claim: The vast majority (>90%) of GWAS associations are driven by non-coding variation.
source: One of the main difficulties in GWAS gene discovery is that the vast majority (>90%) of associations are driven by non-coding variation (Giral et al., 2018; Edwards et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Giral et al., 2018; Edwards et al., 2013.

claim: Transcriptome-wide association studies (TWASs) and expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) colocalization have been developed to leverage transcriptomic data for gene discovery.
source: Over the last decade, approaches such as transcriptome-wide association studies (TWASs) and expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) colocalization have been developed which leverage transcriptomic data in order to inform gene discovery by connecting non-coding disease-associated variants to changes in transcript levels (Gusev et al., 2016; Barbeira et al., 2018; Pividori et al., 2020; Giambartolomei et al., 2014; Wen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gusev et al., 2016; Barbeira et al., 2018; Pividori et al., 2020; Giambartolomei et al., 2014; Wen et al., 2017.

claim: TWAS and eQTL colocalization approaches have proven successful for a wide array of diseases and disease-associated quantitative traits.
source: These approaches have proven successful for a wide array of diseases and disease-associated quantitative traits (Pividori et al., 2020; Bhattacharya et al., 2020; Thom and Voight, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pividori et al., 2020; Bhattacharya et al., 2020; Thom and Voight, 2020.

claim: The osteoporosis field has lagged behind in TWAS/colocalization efforts due to the limited number of large-scale bone-related transcriptomic datasets.
source: However, the osteoporosis field has lagged behind such efforts, due to the limited number of large-scale bone-related transcriptomic datasets.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on the authors' assessment.

claim: The GTEx project has generated RNA-seq data on over 50 tissues across hundreds of individuals.
source: The GTEx project has generated RNA-seq data on over 50 tissues across hundreds of individuals (Consortium, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Consortium, 2020.

claim: Many eQTL are shared across tissues.
source: Even though data on the tissues/cell types likely to be most relevant to BMD (bone or bone cells) were not included, the project demonstrated that many eQTL were shared across tissues (Consortium, 2020; Battle et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Consortium, 2020; Battle et al., 2017.

claim: Effects in a wide-array of non-bone cell types and tissues can impact bone and BMD.
source: Additionally, it is well known that effects in a wide-array of non-bone cell types and tissues can impact bone and BMD (Fitzpatrick, 2002; Mirza and Canalis, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fitzpatrick, 2002; Mirza and Canalis, 2015.

claim: A total of 2156 protein-coding genes were significantly (Bonferroni-adjusted p value ≤0.05) associated with eBMD.
source: A total of 2156 protein-coding genes were significantly (Bonferroni-adjusted p value ≤0.05) associated with eBMD (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the TWAS analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: 1182 colocalizing protein-coding genes were identified with a regional colocalization probability (RCP) of 0.1 or greater.
source: We identified 1182 colocalizing protein-coding genes with a regional colocalization probability (RCP) of 0.1 or greater (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the colocalization analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: 512 protein-coding genes were significant in both the TWAS and eQTL colocalization analyses.
source: In total, 512 protein-coding genes were significant in both the TWAS and eQTL colocalization analyses (Table 1 and Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is a primary finding combining TWAS and colocalization results.

claim: The identified genes included many with well-known roles in the regulation of BMD, such as RUNX2, IGF1, and LRP6.
source: Among the identified genes were many with well-known roles in the regulation of BMD, such as RUNX2 (Figure 1B), IGF1, and LRP6, as well as novel genes such as RERE (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on the list of prioritized genes and known bone biology literature.

claim: The identified genes had significantly colocalizing eQTL in all 49 GTEx tissues.
source: Overall, the identified genes had significantly colocalizing eQTL in all 49 GTEx tissues, with eQTL from cultured fibroblasts (132 genes), subcutaneous adipose tissue (117 genes), tibial artery (115 genes), and tibial nerve (114 genes) exhibiting the highest number of significant colocalizations (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is based on the colocalization analysis results across GTEx tissues.

claim: Of the 1097 autosomal loci, almost half (542; 49%) contained at least one of the 512 prioritized genes.
source: Of the 1097 loci, almost half (542; 49%) of the loci contained at least one of the 512 prioritized genes.
evidence: This is based on mapping prioritized genes to GWAS loci.

claim: Most loci overlapped one gene (mean = 1.7, median = 1).
source: Most loci overlapped one gene (mean = 1.7, median = 1); however, 184 loci overlapped multiple genes, including a locus on Chromosome (Chr.) 20 (lead SNP rs6142137) which contained 9 prioritized genes (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the distribution of prioritized genes across GWAS loci.

claim: Of the 512 prioritized genes, 66 (12.9%) were known bone genes, representing a significant enrichment (odds ratio [OR] = 1.72; p = 1.0 × 10−4).
source: Of the 512 genes identified above, 66 (12.9%) were known bone genes, representing a significant enrichment (odds ratio [OR] = 1.72; p = 1.0 × 10−4) over what would be expected by chance (Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is based on enrichment analysis comparing prioritized genes to a curated list of known bone genes.

claim: Gene Ontology enrichment analysis of the 512 prioritized genes showed enrichments in several bone-relevant ontologies, such as 'ossification' (p = 3.1 × 10−6), 'skeletal system development' (p = 2 × 10−5), and 'regulation of osteoblast differentiation' (p = 3.9 × 10−5).
source: We observed enrichments in several bone-relevant ontologies, such as 'ossification' (p = 3.1 × 10−6), 'skeletal system development' (p = 2 × 10−5), and 'regulation of osteoblast differentiation' (p = 3.9 × 10−5) (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology enrichment analysis results.

claim: Of the 863 genes that were the closest genes to eBMD GWAS associations, 139 were members of the 'known bone gene list', representing a more significant enrichment (OR = 2.56, p = 6.37 × 10−19) than the prioritization approach.
source: Of the 863 genes that were the closest genes to eBMD GWAS associations (Supplementary file 1h), 139 were members of the 'known bone gene list', representing a more significant enrichment of 'known bone genes' than our prioritization approach (OR = 2.56, p = 6.37 × 10−19).
evidence: This is based on comparison of enrichment between the prioritization approach and the closest gene approach.

claim: Of the 512 prioritized genes, 206 (40%) were also the closest genes to eBMD GWAS associations.
source: Of our 512 prioritized genes, 206 (40%) were also the closest genes to eBMD GWAS associations, with 27 of the remaining 306 prioritized genes (8.8%) being members of the 'known bone gene' list.
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis between prioritized genes and closest genes to GWAS associations.

claim: Of the 512 prioritized genes, 142 (27.7%) had been tested by the IMPC.
source: Of the 512, 142 (27.7%) had been tested by the IMPC and 64 (12.5% of the 512 prioritized genes, 45% of the 142 IMPC-tested genes) had a nominally significant (p ≤ 0.05) alteration of whole-body BMD in knockout/knockdown mice, compared to controls.
evidence: This is based on querying the IMPC database for prioritized genes.

claim: 64 of the 512 prioritized genes (12.5%) had a nominally significant (p ≤ 0.05) alteration of whole-body BMD in knockout/knockdown mice.
source: Of the 512, 142 (27.7%) had been tested by the IMPC and 64 (12.5% of the 512 prioritized genes, 45% of the 142 IMPC-tested genes) had a nominally significant (p ≤ 0.05) alteration of whole-body BMD in knockout/knockdown mice, compared to controls.
evidence: This is based on IMPC data for prioritized genes.

claim: Of the 64 genes with significant BMD alterations in IMPC, 49 (76.5%) were not members of the 'known bone gene' list.
source: Of the 64, 49 (76.5%) were not members of the 'known bone gene' list (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is based on comparison of IMPC-validated genes with the known bone gene list.

claim: GPATCH1 is part of the catalytic step 2 spliceosome and may be involved in mRNA splicing.
source: GPATCH1 is part of the catalytic step 2 spliceosome, and may be involved in mRNA splicing, and is predicted to enable RNA-binding activity.
evidence: This is based on known molecular function of GPATCH1.

claim: GPATCH1 is expressed in bone cells in mouse.
source: It is also expressed in bone cells in mouse (Alliance of genome resources, 2022; Lattin et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alliance of genome resources, 2022; Lattin et al., 2008.

claim: GPATCH1 had the strongest TWAS association (p = 3.44 × 10−226) in its genomic region.
source: Of all the genes in the region, GPATCH1 had the strongest TWAS association (p = 3.44 × 10−226) (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is based on TWAS results for the GPATCH1 locus.

claim: GPATCH1 had the strongest eQTL colocalization (whole blood, RCP = 0.36) in its genomic region.
source: and the strongest eQTL colocalization (whole blood, RCP = 0.36) (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is based on colocalization results for the GPATCH1 locus.

claim: The eQTL and BMD GWAS allele effects for the top SNPs in the GPATCH1 locus were in the same direction, suggesting that decreasing the expression of GPATCH1 would lead to decreased BMD.
source: The eQTL and BMD GWAS allele effects for the top SNPs were in the same direction, suggesting that decreasing the expression of GPATCH1 would lead to decreased BMD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the direction of effects in eQTL and GWAS data.

claim: Female mice heterozygous for a Gpatch1 null allele had decreased BMD (p = 2.17 × 10−8).
source: BMD data from the IMPC showed that female mice heterozygous for a Gpatch1 null allele had decreased BMD (p = 2.17 × 10−8) (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on IMPC experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: PPP6R3 is a regulatory subunit of protein phosphatase 6.
source: PPP6R3, a regulatory subunit of protein phosphatase 6, which shows ubiquitous expression across tissues in humans (Cristiano, 2020), is located on human Chr. 11 within 1 Mbp of seven independent eBMD GWAS SNPs identified by Morris et al., 2019 (subsequently referred to as 'eBMD lead SNPs') (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on known molecular function of PPP6R3, supported by citation to Cristiano, 2020.

claim: PPP6R3 shows ubiquitous expression across tissues in humans.
source: PPP6R3, a regulatory subunit of protein phosphatase 6, which shows ubiquitous expression across tissues in humans (Cristiano, 2020), is located on human Chr. 11 within 1 Mbp of seven independent eBMD GWAS SNPs identified by Morris et al., 2019 (subsequently referred to as 'eBMD lead SNPs') (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cristiano, 2020.

claim: PPP6R3 is located on human Chr. 11 within 1 Mbp of seven independent eBMD GWAS SNPs.
source: PPP6R3, a regulatory subunit of protein phosphatase 6, which shows ubiquitous expression across tissues in humans (Cristiano, 2020), is located on human Chr. 11 within 1 Mbp of seven independent eBMD GWAS SNPs identified by Morris et al., 2019 (subsequently referred to as 'eBMD lead SNPs') (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on genomic location data and GWAS results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Of all the protein-coding genes (N = 29) in the ~1.8 Mbp region surrounding PPP6R3, its expression was the most significantly associated with eBMD by TWAS (Bonferroni = 5.7 × 10−93).
source: Of all the protein-coding genes (N = 29) in the ~1.8 Mbp region surrounding PPP6R3, its expression was the most significantly associated with eBMD by TWAS (Bonferroni = 5.7 × 10−93) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on TWAS results for the PPP6R3 locus shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PPP6R3 was the only gene in the region with eQTL that colocalized with at least one of the eBMD associations.
source: Furthermore, PPP6R3 was the only gene in the region with eQTL (in four GTEx tissues, thyroid, ovary, brain_putamen_basal_ganglia, and stomach with RCPs = 0.53, 0.50, 0.28, and 0.14, respectively) that colocalized with at least one of the eBMD associations (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on colocalization analysis results for the PPP6R3 locus shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The most significant PPP6R3 eQTL SNP in thyroid tissue was rs10047483 (Chr. 11, 68.464237 Mbp) (PPP6R3 eQTL p = 6.99 × 10−8, eBMD GWAS p = 1.2 × 10−100).
source: The most significant PPP6R3 eQTL SNP in thyroid tissue (the tissue with the highest RCP) was rs10047483 (Chr. 11, 68.464237 Mbp) (PPP6R3 eQTL p = 6.99 × 10−8, eBMD GWAS p = 1.2 × 10−100) located in intron 1 of PPP6R3.
evidence: This is based on eQTL and GWAS data for the PPP6R3 locus.

claim: The most significant eBMD lead SNP in the PPP6R3 locus was rs11228240 (Chr. 11, 68.450822 Mbp, eBMD GWAS p = 6.6 × 10−101, PPP6R3 eQTL p = 3.7 × 10−6).
source: The most significant eBMD lead SNP in the locus was rs11228240 (Chr. 11, 68.450822 Mbp, eBMD GWAS p = 6.6 × 10−101, PPP6R3 eQTL p = 3.7 × 10−6), located upstream of PPP6R3.
evidence: This is based on GWAS and eQTL data for the PPP6R3 locus.

claim: rs10047483 and rs11228240 are in high LD (r2 = 0.941).
source: Consistent with the colocalization analysis, these two variants are in high LD (r2 = 0.941) and rs10047483 does not exhibit strong LD (r2 < 0.104) with any of the other six eBMD lead SNPs in the locus.
evidence: This is based on LD calculations for SNPs in the PPP6R3 locus.

claim: The eQTL and BMD GWAS allele effects for rs10047483 were opposing, suggesting that a decrease in the expression of PPP6R3 would lead to an increase in BMD.
source: The eQTL and BMD GWAS allele effects for rs10047483 were opposing, suggesting that a decrease in the expression of PPP6R3 would lead to an increase in BMD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the direction of effects in eQTL and GWAS data.

claim: A recent fracture GWAS identified 14 significant associations, one of which was located in the PPP6R3 region (rs35989399, Chr. 11, 68.622433 Mbp).
source: A recent fracture GWAS identified 14 significant associations, one of which was located in the PPP6R3 region (rs35989399, Chr. 11, 68.622433 Mbp) (Morris et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Morris et al., 2019.

claim: PPP6R3 expression when analyzed by TWAS was significant for fracture (TWAS Bonferroni-pval = 6.0 × 10−3).
source: We found that PPP6R3 expression when analyzed by TWAS was significant for fracture (TWAS Bonferroni-pval = 6.0 × 10−3) and the same PPP6R3 eQTL colocalized with the fracture association (RCP = 0.49 in ovary, RCP = 0.36 in thyroid) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on TWAS analysis of fracture GWAS data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The same PPP6R3 eQTL colocalized with the fracture association (RCP = 0.49 in ovary, RCP = 0.36 in thyroid).
source: We found that PPP6R3 expression when analyzed by TWAS was significant for fracture (TWAS Bonferroni-pval = 6.0 × 10−3) and the same PPP6R3 eQTL colocalized with the fracture association (RCP = 0.49 in ovary, RCP = 0.36 in thyroid) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on colocalization analysis of fracture GWAS data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The absence of PPP6R3 protein in MUT mice was confirmed through western blotting.
source: The absence of PPP6R3 protein in MUT mice was confirmed through western blotting (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PPP6R3 was differentially expressed between the mutant and wild-type mice (padj = 3.67 × 10−104, log2 fold change = −1.63).
source: Furthermore, we sequenced RNA extracted from the L5 vertebrae of wild-type and mutant mice, and found that PPP6R3 was differentially expressed between the mutant and wild-type mice (padj = 3.67 × 10−104, log2 fold change = −1.63).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: No changes in gene expression were observed for any other gene in the locus, including Lrp5 (padj = 0.99, log2 fold change = −0.068).
source: We did not observe changes in gene expression for any other gene in the locus, including Lrp5 (padj = 0.99, log2 fold change = −0.068), a well-known regulator of bone mass just upstream of Ppp6r3 (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: In a GWAS by Estrada et al., 2012, a total of 56 loci were identified for femoral neck (FNBMD) and lumbar spine (LSBMD) BMD.
source: In a GWAS by Estrada et al., 2012, a total of 56 loci were identified for femoral neck (FNBMD) and lumbar spine (LSBMD) BMD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Estrada et al., 2012.

claim: One of the 56 loci in the Estrada et al., 2012 GWAS corresponded to the same SNPs associated with the PPP6R3 eQTL.
source: One of the 56 loci corresponded to the same SNPs associated with the PPP6R3 eQTL.
evidence: This is based on comparison of GWAS loci with PPP6R3 eQTL SNPs.

claim: The PPP6R3 locus was significant for LSBMD but did not reach genome-wide significance for FNBMD.
source: The locus was significant for LSBMD; however, it did not reach genome-wide significance for FNBMD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on GWAS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No change in body weight was observed at 9 weeks in Ppp6r3 mice.
source: First, we observed no change in body weight at 9 weeks that might impact bone phenotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on body weight measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: A significant effect of Ppp6r3 genotype on aBMD at the lumbar spine was observed (WT vs. MUT p = 0.01).
source: As the above analysis predicted, we observed a significant effect of Ppp6r3 genotype on aBMD at the lumbar spine (WT vs. MUT p = 0.01, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C), but not the femur (WT vs. MUT p = 0.26, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on DXA measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: No significant effect of Ppp6r3 genotype on aBMD at the femur was observed (WT vs. MUT p = 0.26).
source: As the above analysis predicted, we observed a significant effect of Ppp6r3 genotype on aBMD at the lumbar spine (WT vs. MUT p = 0.01, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C), but not the femur (WT vs. MUT p = 0.26, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on DXA measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Significantly decreased femoral width was observed in Ppp6r3 mutant mice (anterior–posterior [AP] femoral width, WT vs. MUT p = 0.02; medial–lateral [ML] femoral width, WT vs. MUT p = 2.2 × 10−6).
source: It should also be noted, however, that we observed significantly decreased femoral width, but not length, in Ppp6r3 mutant mice (anterior–posterior [AP] femoral width, WT vs. MUT p = 0.02; medial–lateral [ML] femoral width, WT vs. MUT p = 2.2 × 10−6, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is based on caliper measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: Significant decreases in trabecular bone volume fraction (BV/TV, WT vs. MUT p = 0.015) of the lumbar spine were observed as a function of Ppp6r3 genotype.
source: We observed significant (p ≤ 0.05) decreases in trabecular bone volume fraction (BV/TV, WT vs. MUT p = 0.015, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E, F) and volumetric BMD (vBMD, WT vs. MUT p = 0.015, Figure 4—figure supplement 2G) of the lumbar spine as a function of Ppp6r3 genotype
evidence: This is based on μCT measurements shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Significant decreases in volumetric BMD (vBMD, WT vs. MUT p = 0.015) of the lumbar spine were observed as a function of Ppp6r3 genotype.
source: We observed significant (p ≤ 0.05) decreases in trabecular bone volume fraction (BV/TV, WT vs. MUT p = 0.015, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E, F) and volumetric BMD (vBMD, WT vs. MUT p = 0.015, Figure 4—figure supplement 2G) of the lumbar spine as a function of Ppp6r3 genotype
evidence: This is based on μCT measurements shown in Figure 4G.

claim: No significant changes in tissue mineral density (TMD), trabecular separation (TbSp), trabecular thickness (TbTh), or trabecular number (TbN) of the lumbar spine were found.
source: but found no significant changes in tissue mineral density (TMD, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E), trabecular separation (TbSp), trabecular thickness (TbTh), or trabecular number (TbN) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F–H).
evidence: This is based on μCT measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E-H.

claim: Significant decreases in total area (Tot.Ar, WT vs. MUT p = 0.00724) in the femoral midshaft were observed.
source: In the femoral midshaft, we observed significant decreases in total area (Tot.Ar, WT vs. MUT p = 0.00724, Figure 4—figure supplement 2H) and medullary area (Ma.Ar, WT vs. MUT p = 0.00903, Figure 4—figure supplement 2I)
evidence: This is based on μCT measurements shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Significant decreases in medullary area (Ma.Ar, WT vs. MUT p = 0.00903) in the femoral midshaft were observed.
source: In the femoral midshaft, we observed significant decreases in total area (Tot.Ar, WT vs. MUT p = 0.00724, Figure 4—figure supplement 2H) and medullary area (Ma.Ar, WT vs. MUT p = 0.00903, Figure 4—figure supplement 2I)
evidence: This is based on μCT measurements shown in Figure 4I.

claim: No changes in trabecular bone parameters in the distal femur were observed.
source: We did not observe any changes in trabecular bone parameters in the distal femur.
evidence: This is based on μCT measurements of the distal femur.

claim: A significant increase in P1NP levels in mutant mice was observed (p = 0.00422).
source: We also measured Procollagen 1 Intact N-Terminal Propeptide P1NP levels in plasma, and observed a significant increase in P1NP levels in mutant mice (p = 0.00422), suggesting that the observed decrease in bone mass is due to increased bone turnover (Figure 4—figure supplement 2I–K).
evidence: This is based on P1NP measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2I-K.

claim: The observed decrease in bone mass is due to increased bone turnover.
source: We also measured Procollagen 1 Intact N-Terminal Propeptide P1NP levels in plasma, and observed a significant increase in P1NP levels in mutant mice (p = 0.00422), suggesting that the observed decrease in bone mass is due to increased bone turnover (Figure 4—figure supplement 2I–K).
evidence: This is an inference based on P1NP measurements, which is a marker of bone formation.

claim: No significant effects of Ppp6r3 genotype on bone matrix composition were observed.
source: Finally, to assess the effects of Ppp6r3 genotype on bone matrix composition, we performed periosteal Raman spectroscopy on both the lumbar spines and femurs. We did not observe any significant (p ≤ 0.05) effects of Ppp6r3 genotype on bone matrix composition (Figure 4—figure supplements 3–6).
evidence: This is based on Raman spectroscopy measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 3–6.

claim: The lack of differences in bone matrix composition might be due to the fact that relatively young mice were used for these assays.
source: The lack of differences might be due to the fact that we used relatively young mice for these assays.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about why no differences were observed.

claim: The direction of eQTL effects can differ between different cells and tissues within humans.
source: First, our hypothesis was based on expression data in non-bone tissues and cell types. Recent studies have shown that the direction of eQTL effects can differ between different cells and tissues within humans (Peters et al., 2016; Mizuno and Okada, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peters et al., 2016; Mizuno and Okada, 2019.

claim: Many eQTL are shared among tissues.
source: While studies have shown that many eQTL are shared among tissues, the lack of eQTL data in bone and bone cells means that bone-specific eQTL were missed.
evidence: This is based on known properties of eQTL from GTEx and other studies.

claim: A study by Mullin et al. performed eQTL colocalization and summary-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) using GWAS and expression data from osteoclast-like cells.
source: For example, a study conducted by Mullin et al. performed eQTL colocalization and summary-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) by utilizing GWAS and expression data from osteoclast-like cells, and prioritized several eBMD genes (Mullin et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mullin et al., 2020.

claim: Thirty-eight percent of the colocalizing eQTL identified by Mullin et al. overlapped with the 512 prioritized genes in this study.
source: Thirty-eight percent of the colocalizing eQTL and 19% of the SMR genes that they identified overlapped with our 512 prioritized genes, suggesting that we have missed many potential effector genes with eQTL specific to bone cells.
evidence: This is based on comparison of results with Mullin et al., 2020.

claim: Nineteen percent of the SMR genes identified by Mullin et al. overlapped with the 512 prioritized genes in this study.
source: Thirty-eight percent of the colocalizing eQTL and 19% of the SMR genes that they identified overlapped with our 512 prioritized genes, suggesting that we have missed many potential effector genes with eQTL specific to bone cells.
evidence: This is based on comparison of results with Mullin et al., 2020.

claim: The use of multiple non-bone tissues may have inflated the number of false positives based on coincidence of strong TWAS and eQTL colocalization signals that have no biological impact on bone.
